q: For real numbers a and b, exactly one of a < b, a = b or a > b is true. What is this property of real numbers called?
x: Exactly one of the three order relations holds: this is the trichotomy property. Transitivity says a < b and b < c give a < c; closure says an operation keeps results inside the set.

q: Which of these sets is NOT closed under subtraction?
o: the set N of natural numbers
the set Q of rational numbers
the set R of real numbers
x: 2 − 5 = −3 is not a natural number, so N is not closed under subtraction. The difference of two integers, two rationals or two reals stays in the same set.

q: Which fraction equals the recurring decimal 0.3666… (only the 6 repeats)?
x: Let x = 0.3666…; then 100x − 10x = 36.666… − 3.666… = 33, so x = 33/90 = 11/30. Treating both digits as repeating gives 36/99 = 4/11, which is 0.3636…

q: What is (√5 + √3)/(√5 − √3) in simplest form?
x: Multiply top and bottom by √5 + √3: (5 + 3 + 2√15)/(5 − 3) = (8 + 2√15)/2 = 4 + √15. Forgetting to divide by 5 − 3 = 2 gives 8 + 2√15.

q: a and b are rational numbers and a + b√2 = (1 + √2)². What is a + b?
x: (1 + √2)² = 1 + 2√2 + 2 = 3 + 2√2. Since √2 is irrational, the rational parts and the √2 parts must match: a = 3, b = 2, so a + b = 5. Dropping the middle term 2√2 gives 3.

q: What is √(7 + 4√3)?
x: Look for (p + √q)² = p² + q + 2p√q = 7 + 4√3: p = 2, q = 3 works (4 + 3 = 7 and 2·2√3 = 4√3). Check: (2 + √3)² = 7 + 4√3, while (1 + 2√3)² = 13 + 4√3. Taking roots term by term (√7 + √4) is the usual slip.

q: What is the additive inverse of the complex number −2 + 5i?
x: The additive inverse w satisfies z + w = 0, so w = −z = 2 − 5i. −2 − 5i is the conjugate and (−2 − 5i)/29 is the multiplicative inverse.

q: x and y are real numbers and (2x − y) + (x + y)i = 4 + 5i. What are x and y?
x: Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts: 2x − y = 4 and x + y = 5. Adding gives 3x = 9, so x = 3 and y = 2. Check: 6 − 2 = 4 and 3 + 2 = 5.

q: Which statement is true for all complex numbers z₁ and z₂?
o: the conjugate of z₁z₂ equals z̄₁·z̄₂
x: Conjugation respects products: the conjugate of z₁z₂ is z̄₁z̄₂. The others fail: for z₁ = 1, z₂ = i, |1 + i| = √2 ≠ 2 and |1 − i| = √2 ≠ 0; for z₁ = z₂ = i, Re(i·i) = −1 but Re(i)·Re(i) = 0.

q: If z = 2 − 3i, what is z² − 4z?
For which real number k is (k + 2i)/(1 − i) a real number?
x: Multiply top and bottom by 1 + i: (k + 2i)(1 + i)/2 = ((k − 2) + (k + 2)i)/2. This is real when k + 2 = 0, so k = −2 (the number is then −2). k = 2 makes it purely imaginary instead.

q: Complex numbers z₁ and z₂ satisfy |z₁| = 3, |z₂| = 4 and |z₁ + z₂| = 5. What is |z₁ − z₂|?
x: |z₁ + z₂|² + |z₁ − z₂|² = 2(|z₁|² + |z₂|²) = 2(9 + 16) = 50, so |z₁ − z₂|² = 50 − 25 = 25 and |z₁ − z₂| = 5. Check with z₁ = 3, z₂ = 4i: |3 + 4i| = 5 and |3 − 4i| = 5.

q: Writing complex numbers as ordered pairs, what is (3, −2) + (−1, 5)?
x: Ordered pairs add component by component: (3 + (−1), −2 + 5) = (2, 3). In the usual form this is (3 − 2i) + (−1 + 5i) = 2 + 3i.

q: z₁ = 2(cos 40° + i sin 40°) and z₂ = 3(cos 20° + i sin 20°). What is z₁z₂ in the form a + bi?
x: Multiply the moduli and add the arguments: z₁z₂ = 6(cos 60° + i sin 60°) = 6(½ + (√3/2)i) = 3 + 3√3 i. Adding the moduli instead gives 5/2 + (5√3/2)i; swapping cos and sin gives 3√3 + 3i.

q: In the Argand diagram, the points z with |z − 2 + i| = 3 form a circle. What are its centre and radius?
x: |z − 2 + i| = |z − (2 − i)| is the distance of z from 2 − i, so the circle has centre (2, −1) and radius 3. Reading the signs straight off gives (−2, 1); 9 is the square of the radius.

q: A complex number has modulus 2√2 and argument π/4. What is it?
x: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = 2√2(1/√2 + i/√2) = 2 + 2i. Check: |2 + 2i| = √8 = 2√2, and the point (2, 2) lies on the line y = x in the first quadrant.

q: In the Argand diagram, z = 3 + 4i. What is the area of the triangle with vertices z, iz and z + iz?
x: iz is z turned through 90°, so O, z, z + iz and iz are the corners of a square of side |z| = 5. The triangle is half of that square: ½ × 25 = 25/2. Check with the points (3, 4), (−4, 3), (−1, 7): ½|3(3 − 7) − 4(7 − 4) − 1(4 − 3)| = 25/2.

q: What is the smallest positive integer n for which ((1 + i)/√2)ⁿ = 1?
x: (1 + i)/√2 = cos 45° + i sin 45°, so by De Moivre's theorem its nth power is cos 45n° + i sin 45n°. This is 1 when 45n is a multiple of 360, first at n = 8. At n = 4 it is cos 180° = −1.

q: A quadratic equation with real coefficients has 3 − 2i as one root. What is the other root?
x: Non-real roots of a quadratic with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs, so the other root is 3 + 2i. Together they give the real equation x² − 6x + 13 = 0 (sum 6, product 9 + 4 = 13).

q: a and b are real, a > 0, and (a + bi)² = −7 − 24i. What is b?
x: a² − b² = −7 and 2ab = −24, so b = −12/a and a⁴ + 7a² − 144 = 0, giving a² = 9, a = 3 and b = −4. Check: (3 − 4i)² = 9 − 24i − 16 = −7 − 24i. The sign of b must match the sign of 2ab = −24.

q: Which quadratic equation has the roots 3 + i and 3 − i?
x: Sum of roots = 6 and product = (3 + i)(3 − i) = 9 + 1 = 10, so the equation is x² − 6x + 10 = 0. Taking the product as 9 − 1 = 8 is the usual slip.

q: One root of x² − (2 + i)x + (1 + i) = 0 is 1. What is the other root?
x: The sum of the roots is 2 + i, so the other root is (2 + i) − 1 = 1 + i. Check with the product: 1 × (1 + i) = 1 + i, the constant term. The coefficients are not real, so the conjugate 1 − i need not be a root.

q: How many complex numbers z satisfy z² = z̄ (the conjugate of z)?
x: Taking moduli, |z|² = |z|, so |z| = 0 or 1. z = 0 works; if |z| = 1 then z̄ = 1/z, so z³ = 1, giving z = 1, ω or ω². In all 4 solutions: 0, 1, ω, ω². Forgetting z = 0 gives 3.

q: Which of these is a root of x⁴ + 4 = 0?
x: (1 + i)² = 2i and (2i)² = −4, so (1 + i)⁴ + 4 = 0. In fact x⁴ + 4 = (x² − 2x + 2)(x² + 2x + 2), with roots ±1 ± i. By contrast (√2 i)⁴ = 4 and (2i)⁴ = 16.
